sourceText: On night 2, the course began with a prohibition: no one was allowed to solve the problem before they could describe who would pay for the solution. Only then did Aster open the CHILDREN-WORKSHOP sector. The children test their technical right to hide memories and processes from the creator who can read almost every other system. The memorial bore the name of Vinge; Egan; Banks precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. In this part of the course, the real object was not the world being visited but the relation between a creator and what the creator claims to have made for another being’s good. Orin perceived counterfactual costs as absences with weight. He did not confuse an unrealized branch with a victim, but he refused to let success rewrite rejected options as if they had been inevitable all along. Sael was the first inhabitant to contradict them. Sael had neither access to their archives nor any interest in hyperdimensional pedagogy; there was a local problem, with deadlines, relatives, and 41 consequences. For Sael, the speculative mechanism was not an ‘idea.’ It was the environment in which one had to decide what one was willing to risk losing. The problem closed quickly around them: Aster experiences every private region as a physical absence, while Vela insists that opacity must be irreversible without their consent. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Fo — Finitely Extensible: the system remains finite yet extensible; Ps — Substrate-Independent Person: identity is a pattern rather than privileged material. Course references included outfinite motif; Greg Egan — Permutation City. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Orin broke the first consensus. ‘I do not want the perfect branch. I want us to know what we sacrificed in order to call it perfect.’ Marae answered without raising their voice: ‘Do not tell me what their model prefers. Ask them, and bear the time their answer takes.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. For Aster, the pain came not from too few worlds but from the fact that too many had become transparent. She could build variations faster than a human could formulate desires, but calculated 42 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS variation did not produce exteriority. It was like trying to surprise yourself by moving objects around your own room with your eyes closed. Marae remained in the local body when the others opened their protections. The gesture cost her: she felt cold, pressure, and physiological delay at exactly the scale the inhabitants felt them. “Otherwise we risk confusing the fact that we survive with the claim that the situation is bearable,” she said after catching her breath. The night did not end in victory. The Table's first moral lesson becomes this: what can be known only by destroying autonomy is not knowledge one is legitimately entitled to obtain. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. Tern remained a few seconds after the others. A very faint deviation repeated in the sector’s background noise, too coherent to be thermal and too useless to be a teaching signal. He did not tell Aster. It was the first thing he possessed solely by not sharing it. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the SUBSTITUTION operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — replaces the substrate, carrier, or medium of a function — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. 43 Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. When the threshold closed, Aster remained silent one second longer than protocol required. The children had already noticed that this was her smallest unit of fear. 44 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
